messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stress: Stress, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Daniel Reyes had been a school counselor in a public middle school in the suburbs of a large North American city for six years when the accident happened, a role that fit the patient he had always thought of himself as being: steady, patient, good in a crisis. He was married, well-liked by staff and students, and used to being the person others came to when something had gone wrong. The trauma that later reorganized his life occurred on an ordinary afternoon while he was driving home after work. A sudden moment of inattention at an intersection led to a collision that seriously injured another driver, and from the first report onward Daniel was faced with the fact that his own action had been the immediate cause. The details of the scene remained fixed in him with a force that was not limited to memory. In the days after, the police came, questions were asked, and the word “serious” attached itself to the injury in a way he could not shake. He began to avoid police altogether, crossing streets early or changing routes if he saw a cruiser parked near the school or outside a store, because being near them brought back the fear of being asked again to explain what he had done.

In the months that followed, Daniel found that stress itself became a trigger. Staff meetings, paperwork deadlines, noisy afternoons in the counseling office, even the pressure of being asked to handle multiple student crises could send him abruptly back to the accident scene. Medical procedures were another potent cue. When he had to undergo a routine medical examination, the smell of the clinic and the sight of gloves and equipment were enough to make his chest tighten and his body go rigid, as if he were once again watching the injured person being assessed and not yet knowing how badly they were hurt. He noticed that certain smells could bring everything back with startling immediacy. The odor of antiseptic or rubber, or other related smells he encountered in medical settings, would arrive before he had time to prepare, and he would feel suddenly trapped in the original moment, his stomach dropping as if the day of the crash had opened up under him.

What Daniel described most vividly was how the memory came back. It did not feel like something that had happened and ended; it felt present, as though the event was unfolding in front of him again. He could recall the crash, the sound, the impact, and the aftermath across all his senses at once, so fully that for a moment he would be disoriented by the ordinary room around him. He knew what happened, but when he tried to explain it he often found he could not find the words. In sessions he would start, stop, and restart, saying only that it was “the worst thing” and then falling silent, because the experience resisted being shaped into language. At times, the recollection was accompanied by strong physical reactions: his heart would pound, his body would tense, and he would feel flushed and shaken when something reminded him of it. The emotional tone was equally intense, a heavy mix of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame that could arrive without warning and sit in him for hours.

Daniel had come to believe that he could not trust himself to do the right thing. Before the accident, he had seen himself as careful and responsible; afterward, he looked back on his own choices with suspicion and self-reproach, convinced that the event happened because of the way he acted. He repeated to himself that if he had been more attentive, more disciplined, more worthy of the role people expected from him, none of it would have happened. Over time he began to speak about his life as though it had been destroyed by the trauma, not in a dramatic or theatrical way, but with a flat certainty that his future had narrowed around one irreversible mistake. He stayed mentally occupied all the time, keeping himself busy from morning until night, filling gaps with work tasks, errands, news, and scrolling on his phone so there would be less room for thinking about the event. When silence came, or when he was alone at night, the memory pressed in harder, and he would lie awake needing to stay alert, unwilling to let himself drift into sleep quickly because sleep felt like a surrender to whatever might come next in his mind. His marriage had become quieter and more strained, not from open conflict but because he was so often elsewhere in his thoughts, and his wife had begun to notice how often he seemed tense, distracted, and unreachable.

By the time he sought help, Daniel had exhausted his usual ways of getting through the day. He came to treatment because the effort of staying occupied, avoiding police, and steering clear of reminders had become difficult to maintain while continuing to work in a school full of unpredictable stressors and constant demands. He was most afraid that one wrong moment, one lapse in attention or one unexpected reminder, could bring back the full force of the crash or prove that his judgment could never be trusted again. At the same time, he was hoping for some way to live with the memory without feeling as though he were back at the intersection every time it surfaced.
